title: Agent Workflows in Finance

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Drafting Proposal Responses
children.blurb: Drafting proposal responses in finance covers the preparation of written answers to requests for proposals, due diligence questionnaires, and client or counterparty asks in banking, asset management, insurance, and adjacent services.

children.name: Agent Negotiation in Over-the-Counter Markets
children.blurb: Agent negotiation in over-the-counter markets covers automated bilateral bargaining between software agents acting for dealers, asset managers, or corporate treasuries in instruments that trade off exchange, such as corporate bonds, interest rate swaps, foreign exchange forwards, and structured products.

children.name: Investment Committee Memos
children.blurb: Investment committee memos are formal documents that summarize a proposed investment, the analysis behind it, and the decision requested from the committee.

children.name: Keeping Comparable Company Sets Current
children.blurb: Keeping comparable company sets current means maintaining a peer group for valuation or benchmarking so that it reflects each company's present business mix, size, geography, and sector.

children.name: Automating Trade Settlement
children.blurb: Automating trade settlement covers the post-trade steps that move a trade from execution to final exchange of cash and securities, including trade matching, confirmation, reconciliation, settlement instruction generation, and exception handling.

sections.body: Agent workflows in finance use software that can take multi-step actions with limited human oversight across document drafting, market negotiation, internal reporting, data maintenance and post-trade processing. In practice, AI now drafts first versions of responses to requests for proposals by pulling from past submissions and product databases. It also runs scripted negotiation loops in some over-the-counter markets, where a model proposes, counters and logs terms within pre-set boundaries. Investment banks and asset managers use language models to assemble initial committee memos from portfolio data and meeting notes. Comparable company sets are refreshed by agents that scrape filings and update valuation multiples, and settlement teams use rule-based agents to match trade details and flag breaks.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Drafting and summarization are the most mature, with systems producing usable drafts that still require human review for accuracy and tone. Negotiation agents operate in narrow, structured settings, often with hard limits on price and size, and they cannot handle novel or ambiguous counterparty behavior. Memo generation is reliable for formatting and pulling standard figures but not for the final investment judgment. Comparable company updates are partly automated but still break when companies change names, report unusual items or file late. Settlement automation is well established for matching and reconciliation, yet exceptions, failed trades and regulatory escalations still need people. The honest limit is that these agents are not autonomous decision makers, they are workflow tools that reduce repetitive work and surface errors.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader looking at the first step of a deal process would start with Drafting Proposal Responses, which shows how agents assemble and revise client-facing documents. Agent Negotiation in Over-the-Counter Markets covers the more constrained use of models in price and term discussions, and it connects to Automating Trade Settlement because a negotiated trade must eventually be confirmed and settled. Investment Committee Memos sits between research and decision, showing how agents turn portfolio and market data into a structured internal document. Keeping Comparable Company Sets Current supports both proposals and memos by maintaining the valuation inputs those documents rely on. Automating Trade Settlement closes the loop, describing the post-trade agents that match, reconcile and flag exceptions after a trade is agreed.
